analysis.one_liner: Makes enhanced ACA health insurance subsidies permanent and repeals recent Medicaid and Medicare cuts.
analysis.headline: The bill has 141 cosponsors, all Democrats, and has sat in two House committees with no hearing or vote since its August 2025 introduction.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would make permanent the enhanced Affordable Care Act premium tax credits — the subsidies that lower monthly health insurance premiums for people buying coverage on their own — which under current law are scheduled to shrink back at the end of 2025. It would remove the income cap that cuts people off from help above 400% of the poverty line and increase the subsidy amount at every income level. It would also repeal several health provisions of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, including tighter Medicaid eligibility checks and a shorter window for retroactive Medicaid coverage.
analysis.who_benefits: People who buy their own health insurance through the ACA marketplaces would pay lower premiums, and people earning above 400% of the poverty line — currently ineligible for any subsidy — would become eligible. Medicaid enrollees would benefit from restored eligibility rules and a longer window for retroactive coverage. Hospitals and providers would see less unpaid care.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Marketplace insurance buyers and Medicaid enrollees

how_it_helps.text: The bill permanently removes the 400% of federal poverty level income cap on premium tax credit eligibility, so higher-income households buying marketplace coverage can qualify for help again.
It lowers the 'applicable percentages' that determine how much of a premium each household must pay, increasing the subsidy amount across all income tiers, with no cap above 400% of poverty.

It repeals several One Big Beautiful Bill Act health provisions, including certain Medicare and Medicaid eligibility and verification requirements, the shortened window for retroactive Medicaid coverage, and premium tax credit verification requirements.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through higher government spending on the expanded subsidies and the reversal of savings from the repealed Medicaid and Medicare provisions. The bill text contains no offsetting taxes or spending cuts to pay for this.

drawbacks.text: Making the expanded credits permanent with no expiration date and no income cap adds ongoing federal spending with no offsetting revenue in the bill, increasing deficits.

Extending full subsidy eligibility to households above 400% of the poverty line directs some federal dollars to households that could afford coverage without help, a cost an honest supporter must weigh against the middle-class premium relief it provides.

Repealing the premium tax credit and Medicaid verification requirements that the One Big Beautiful Bill Act added removes checks the earlier law's authors argued were needed to prevent improper payments and ineligible enrollment.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the millions of households whose marketplace premiums would roughly double when the enhanced credits lapse, the bill's benefit is large and immediate. The honest cost is fiscal: a permanent, uncapped entitlement with no way to pay for it, including subsidies reaching well above middle-class incomes. A more targeted extension would protect low- and middle-income households at a lower price; this version chooses the broadest expansion.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced on August 1, 2025, referred to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce committees, and has sat in committee without a hearing, markup, or floor vote since.

narrative.text: Rep. Adam Gray introduced the bill on August 1, 2025, and it was referred to the Committee on Ways and Means and, in addition, the Committee on Energy and Commerce.
141 House members cosponsored the bill, all of them Democrats; no Republicans signed on.
The action history shows no further action after the initial referral — no committee vote, no floor vote, and no Senate companion action.
Under current law the enhanced premium tax credits are scheduled to lapse after 2025, meaning the protections this bill would extend are set to expire unless Congress acts separately.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has gone nowhere, current law stands as it is: the One Big Beautiful Bill Act's health provisions remain in effect and the enhanced marketplace subsidies are still set to expire after 2025. Federal budget savings are preserved for now, while marketplace customers face the scheduled premium increases unless Congress passes something else.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: No one gained; current law and its sunset stand

against.what_they_did: No Republican member cosponsored the bill, and the majority's committees have not moved it; the bill would reverse health provisions the majority enacted earlier in 2025.

sides.party_line_note: All 141 cosponsors are Democrats and the sponsor is a Democrat; no Republicans signed on, and the Republican-run committees have not scheduled action.

industries.note: Premium tax credits are paid to insurers selling marketplace plans, so permanently expanding and enlarging the credits locks in a large, permanent stream of subsidized customers for the insurance industry. The repeal of premium tax credit verification requirements also reduces the paperwork insurers face. In this bill the industry's revenue growth travels with consumers' lower premiums.

Repealing the shortened retroactive Medicaid coverage window and tightened Medicaid eligibility and verification requirements would restore coverage for enrollees and reduce the amount of unpaid care hospitals absorb. Providers' interest here runs alongside enrollees' interest in keeping coverage.

analysis.trajectory: With a Republican House majority, two committees that have shown no movement in months, and zero Republican cosponsors, the bill's near-certain path is to die in committee when this Congress ends in January 2027. Its realistic function is as a statement of the Democratic position ahead of the scheduled expiration of the enhanced premium tax credits, which may be taken up instead in a broader bipartisan deal or not at all.
